idiom_name: XCTestCase subclass with setUp and XCTAssert* assertions
implementation_notes: XCTest frames the fixture as the test class: subclass XCTestCase, prepare the arrange beat in setUp()/setUpWithError() with tearDown() for cleanup, and give each behaviour its own test method whose body performs the act and ends with XCTAssertEqual/XCTAssertTrue. A fresh instance is created for every test method, which keeps tests independent, and a failure records the file and line of the macro, so each expectation is one call in the assert beat.
pitfalls: Implicitly unwrapped optional fixtures (var account: Account!) fail at the act beat when setup did not run or threw; setUpWithError() plus explicit handling keeps an arrange failure where it belongs.
XCTAssert* take autoclosures, so a side-effecting call placed inside the expectation runs only when the assertion is evaluated, which can hide the act from the failure report.
An un-awaited Task in an async test can finish after the test ends, so XCTest reports a pass while the act's effect was never verified.

variants.name: Swift Testing @Test with #expect
variants.implementation_notes: Swift Testing replaces the XCTest class with an annotated function: @Test declares the test (or @Suite groups them), the arrange beat is ordinary code, one call is the act, and #expect/#require capture the asserted expression and report its sub-values on failure. It ships with Xcode 16 and later and can coexist with XCTest in the same target, so new unit tests can adopt it while UI and performance tests stay on XCTest.
pitfalls: #expect captures the whole expression, so putting the act call inside it merges the act and assert beats; assign the result first and assert on the value.
#require aborts the test on failure like a precondition, so cleanup written after it does not run - use it only when the rest of the test depends on the condition.
Tests and suites run in parallel in-process, so mutable shared fixtures race; keep the arrange beat local or isolate shared state in an actor.
